title: What's Next?
hook: Ernest Amory Codman tracked his own surgical failures and presented them in public. His hospital found this less comfortable than prestige, and showed him the door. The system he built, following patients for years and recording complications, failures, and their causes, became the foundation of modern surgical outcome auditing. The lesson his career teaches is not about surgery. It is about what happens to accountability systems when accuracy and institutional comfort are in conflict: the institution wins in the short term, and the accountability system wins in the long run only if someone insists on keeping score anyway.
counterintuition: Scorekeeping makes the gap between persuasive and accurate forecasting visible. Without it, the gap is invisible, and institutions reliably default to rewarding the forecaster who sounds most useful rather than the one who turns out to be most right. A scorekeeping system is therefore both the technical improvement mechanism and the institutional threat: it threatens every reputation built on persuasiveness that has never been checked against outcomes.
tryThisNow: Pick one prediction that you or your organization will make publicly in the next six months, a project completion, a sales forecast, a policy outcome. Break it into three component sub-questions, each with its own trackable indicator and checkpoint date. Write these three sub-questions down. These are what accountable forecasting looks like: not the headline number, but the component questions that let you tell the difference between 'we were wrong' and 'the world changed under us.'
keyTakeaway: Scorekeeping converts a forecast into evidence. Without it, accuracy and persuasiveness are indistinguishable, and institutions reward whichever sounds better. A testable question is as important as a careful answer.

breakdown.fastRead:
The foundation program officer slides a grant renewal form across the table and asks: 'What does success look like at twelve months, and how will you measure it?'

Luke has been running the employment re-entry program for six years. She has testimonials, cohort stories, and a waiting list. She does not have twelve-month employment retention data.

She builds the tracking system that quarter. It follows participants for a full year after placement, records whether they are still employed at months three, six, and twelve, and asks why if they are not. She knows the system might show that her program is weaker than the testimonials suggest.

The first cohort's twelve-month data comes back at 61 percent retention.

She had expected 75 percent, based on the testimonials and the cases she knew best. The 14-point gap was a signal about which part of the program was losing people. She presents the 61 percent publicly and redesigns the job-coaching component.

The 61 percent was not a failure. It was a number she could work with. The testimony had only been a number she could present.
breakdown.deepRead:
Ernest Amory Codman tracked his own failures and presented them in public. The hospital found this less comfortable than prestige, and he was shown the door, which tells you more about how institutions treat accountability than about whether his system worked.

At the turn of the 20th century, Codman kept what he called an End Result System. He followed his surgical patients for years after their procedures. He recorded outcomes, noted problems, and wrote down the cases where his judgment had been wrong. He then presented these records, including his failures, at medical society meetings. His colleagues saw this as an attack on surgery as a profession. His hospital found the transparency unsettling. He was asked to leave.

The End Result System became the foundation of modern surgical outcome auditing.

The lesson is not that institutions are malicious. A measure that can prove you wrong is more threatening to an old institution than one that can only confirm what is already believed. When scoring is absent, accuracy and appeal are hard to tell apart. When scoring arrives, reputations built on unchecked appeal are exposed to a test they had been protected from.

That exposure is what Codman's colleagues were actually resisting.
breakdown.fullRead:
The superforecaster solves half the problem. The other half is the question.

A forecast is only as accountable as the question that prompted it. A question that is too vague to score, one that can be interpreted as correct regardless of the outcome, is not a forecasting question: it is a position. The superquestioner who frames a question precisely enough to be checkable is doing work as important as the forecaster who answers it. Without the question being well-formed, even accurate forecasting cannot be detected as such.

Decomposition is the main tool. A five-year chronic disease reduction target is a question that cannot be checked until year five, by which time the intervention window for year-one problems has long closed. Breaking it into annual leading indicators transforms a single unfalsifiable question into five component questions, each of which is checkable, each of which can trigger an early intervention if it goes wrong. Min's department discovered a treatment initiation shortfall in year one that would have been invisible until year five without the intermediate milestones. The decomposition did not change the target. It changed when accountability was real.

A forecast without a score is not a forecast. It is a position. The score is what converts the position into evidence.

The institutional resistance to scorekeeping is not irrational from the perspective of the people who resist it. A public accuracy record is a record of being wrong as often as you are right. A forecaster whose track record shows 71 percent directional accuracy and 90 percent stated confidence has been overconfident for years. Hanna's private spreadsheet kept that information invisible. Making it public would change what her forecasts were worth. The colleagues who resisted her proposal were not protecting incompetence. They were protecting reputations built without accountability, which is a different and more defensible position.

Codeman was forced to leave by a system that preferred comfortable prestige to uncomfortable accuracy. The system he built survived him and eventually transformed the field. That sequence, the inventor of accountability rejected by the institution, the system outlasting its opponents, is probably what improvement in forecasting will look like at scale. Not a sudden embrace of scorekeeping, but a persistent insistence on keeping score anyway, in public, with specificity, until the accumulated evidence is too large to dismiss.

examples.title: Luke implements 12-month employment retention tracking; the first cohort returns 61%, not 75%, and she redesigns a program component

planSpec.domain: nonprofit program director implementing outcome tracking that could prove her own flagship program wrong
planSpec.audience: program director with six years of anecdotal success but no longitudinal outcome tracking
planSpec.stakes: the next funding cycle and organizational credibility with an outcomes-focused foundation funder
planSpec.requiredBeat: director implements 12-month tracking; first cohort returns 61%, not expected 75%; she presents it publicly and redesigns a component

examples.scenario:
'What does success look like at twelve months, and how will you measure it?' The foundation program officer has the grant renewal form open and is waiting.

Luke has six years of testimonials and a waiting list. She does not have an answer to this question in the form the officer is asking for.

She builds the 12-month employment retention tracking system over the following quarter. The system is straightforward: contact each participant at months three, six, and twelve to record employment status, and ask why if they are not working. She knows before she builds it that the results might contradict what the testimonials suggest. She builds it anyway.

The first cohort's data returns nine months later. Employment retention at twelve months: 61 percent. She had estimated, based on the cases she knew and the testimonials she had collected, that the number would be closer to 75 percent.

The 14-point gap pointed directly at the job-coaching component. Participants who completed the program's job-coaching module had 79 percent twelve-month retention. Participants who had attended fewer than two-thirds of the sessions had 44 percent retention. The module attendance rate was lower than the program's records had suggested.

Luke presents the 61 percent figure to the foundation at the next quarterly meeting. She brings the component-level breakdown. She announces a redesign of the job-coaching module's attendance protocol.

The foundation renews the grant at a higher level than before.
examples.whatToDo: Before your next program review or project retrospective, define what a negative result would look like: not 'we didn't achieve the goal,' but specifically which component, at which milestone, would show that something was not working. Build the measurement system that would detect that specific signal. If you cannot define the negative result in advance, you cannot distinguish between 'the program works' and 'the program has not yet been tested.'
examples.whyItMatters: Luke's six years of testimonials were real. They were also a selected sample. The 12-month retention tracking system produced a number she had not chosen and could not have predicted, which is the only kind of number that contains diagnostic information. The 61 percent was not a failure: it was the first accurate reading of where the program actually stood, and the first number specific enough to redesign from.

examples.title: Hanna discovers a 71% accuracy rate hidden in a private spreadsheet and proposes the departmental forecast log her colleagues resist

planSpec.domain: government policy analyst making her prediction accuracy record public
planSpec.audience: senior analyst with eight years of policy impact forecasts and no structured accuracy review
planSpec.stakes: departmental credibility and professional standing in a culture without current forecast tracking
planSpec.requiredBeat: analyst finds 71% accuracy vs 90%+ confidence gap; proposes departmental forecast log; three colleagues resist

examples.scenario:
The spreadsheet has been in a folder labeled 'personal review' for five years. Hanna opens it on a Thursday afternoon to find a row she started adding to in 2019 and never shared: her own forecast log.

Each row has a date, a claim, a confidence level, and a column for the outcome once it was clear. She has 87 entries. She scores them that afternoon.

Her directional accuracy: 71 percent. Her average stated confidence on the forecasts she got right: 88 percent. Her average stated confidence on the forecasts she got wrong: 85 percent. There is almost no difference between how confident she felt about her accurate predictions and how confident she felt about her inaccurate ones.

She has been systematically overconfident for years.

She drafts a proposal for a departmental forecast log: a shared document where all policy impact forecasts would be recorded with stated confidence levels, trackable outcomes, and a quarterly accuracy review. The proposal would make the review public within the department.

Three colleagues tell her separately that the proposal is premature. One says the measurement would be used unfairly by management. One says forecasts in this domain are too complex to score reliably. One asks whether there is any evidence that tracking improves outcomes.

Hanna notes that all three colleagues make frequent verbal forecasts that have never been written down. The department head's weekly check-in is tomorrow morning. Hanna is deciding whether to submit the proposal before the weekly check-in and let the objections surface in real time, or wait for a softer opening. She submits it that evening, knowing the objections will be on the table by noon.
examples.whatToDo: Keep your own forecast log before proposing a shared one. Record each significant prediction with a date, a stated confidence level, and a resolution column. Review it quarterly. The patterns in your own log, especially the gap between stated confidence and actual accuracy, are the argument you will need when proposing institutional-level tracking to people who have never seen their own record.
examples.whyItMatters: Hanna's three resistant colleagues were protecting something real: reputations built in an environment without accountability. Their objections were not dishonest, but they mapped onto the positions of people whose track records had never been made comparable. The departmental forecast log would have created a comparison that their verbal forecasting careers had been protected from.

examples.title: Pablo breaks a single annual revenue forecast into five component questions; the board can finally diagnose rather than just observe the miss

planSpec.domain: corporate strategy team decomposing an oversized annual growth question into auditable component forecasts
planSpec.audience: strategy team with six years of single-number annual forecasts that have been revised repeatedly mid-year
planSpec.stakes: board credibility when the number is consistently revised; board cannot tell whether the forecast was wrong or the world changed
planSpec.requiredBeat: five-component decomposition; first quarterly review shows 2/5 on track and 3/5 off; board can diagnose rather than observe

examples.scenario:
It is a Tuesday in early December. You are a senior strategist at a mid-size technology company, preparing the annual planning package that the board will review in January. You have been watching the same pattern for three years. A single annual revenue number is issued in January. By April, conditions have changed and it is revised. By August, it is revised again. The board asks, every time, whether the original forecast was wrong or whether something unexpected changed. The team gives a nuanced answer. The board gets neither a clear diagnosis nor a way to check.

Consider what Pablo proposes. He breaks the annual revenue forecast into five component questions: volume per segment, price realization, new logo conversion rate, renewal rate, and market expansion rate. Each component has its own probability estimate. Each has a quarterly checkpoint. Each is specific enough to score independently.

At the first quarterly review, two components are on track and three are not. Price realization and renewal rate are at or above forecast. New logo conversion, volume in the mid-market segment, and market expansion are all below.

The board can now distinguish between 'the world changed' and 'the forecast was wrong in specific areas.' New logo conversion has been below forecast for three quarters and the trend is structural. Market expansion missed because a regulatory change in one geography pushed the timeline by six months.

These are different diagnoses. They require different responses. A single number that missed by 8% would have required a response to 8%, with no ability to direct it. You must decide before submitting the January package whether to propose the five-component structure to the board, which will require explaining why the old format was inadequate, or keep the familiar single-number format and accept another year of undiagnosable misses.
examples.whatToDo: When issuing a large aggregate forecast, break it into component sub-questions before the forecast period begins. Each component should have: a specific claim, a trackable indicator, and a checkpoint date. The components are what make early intervention possible and what make post-period diagnosis coherent rather than post-hoc.
examples.whyItMatters: Pablo's five-component structure did not make the forecast more accurate in the first year. It made the miss diagnosable. A diagnosable miss is more useful than an accurate forecast for the purpose of improving the next one: it tells the team which of their models was wrong, not just that the total was wrong.

examples.title: Devon reviews 140 expert predictions across three years, scores 68, finds a 74-to-46 percent accuracy spread, and proposes ranking contributors publicly

planSpec.domain: journalism editor tracking reporter prediction accuracy over three years
planSpec.audience: managing editor whose publication frequently publishes expert predictions
planSpec.stakes: reader trust and the ability to differentiate expert contributors from competitors'
planSpec.requiredBeat: 140 predictions tracked; 68 scoreable; 74% vs 46% spread found; contributor ranking proposal meets resistance from low-accuracy contributors

examples.scenario:
Devon had started the back-issue review as a project about sourcing. She tagged every prediction made under a named expert byline over three years, 140 total across political, economic, and market coverage. She had not intended to score them. She scored them anyway.

Of the 140 tagged predictions, 72 could not be evaluated: the claim was too vague, the outcome had not resolved, or the prediction was structured as a question rather than a claim. Of the 68 that could be scored, the spread was wider than she expected.

The top-performing contributor was correct 74 percent of the time on directional claims. The lowest-performing was correct 46 percent of the time, which is below the 50 percent rate a random assignment of confident-sounding predictions would have achieved.

Devon must decide whether to bring the accuracy findings to the editorial board and propose public contributor rankings, knowing the two lowest-performing contributors will likely object, or report the findings privately and let the editors act on the information without making the rankings public.

She proposes the public rankings. The two contributors with the lowest accuracy records sent objections within the week. Their argument: accuracy metrics do not capture the analytical value of their work, which lies in the depth of reasoning rather than the directional outcome. The top-performing contributor did not object.

Devon published the ranking for the first year. The two low-accuracy contributors remained contributors but their placement in the publication changed.
examples.whatToDo: If your organization publishes predictions or impact estimates from named contributors, run a backward scoring exercise on the past three years. Score only the predictions specific enough to evaluate. The ratio of scoreable to total predictions will tell you how much of your expert content is actually accountable, and the accuracy spread will tell you what differentiating contributors by track record would look like.
examples.whyItMatters: Devon's 72 unscorable predictions were not meaningless. They had performed a function: they appeared authoritative and could not be shown to be wrong. The 68 scoreable predictions revealed a 28-percentage-point spread in accuracy between the publication's best and worst contributors. That spread had been invisible because no one had checked. Making it visible changed what contributor reputation meant at the publication.

examples.title: Lukas asks the negative-result question no one raised and the committee discovers the study design cannot detect a null finding

planSpec.domain: university research review board member asking the obvious but neglected framing question about a study design
planSpec.audience: grant review committee reviewing an institutional grant application for a behavioral intervention study
planSpec.stakes: $850K in institutional grant funding; study design will determine whether results can be interpreted
planSpec.requiredBeat: one member asks 'what would a negative result look like?'; design is discovered to be one-sided by accident; application returned for redesign

examples.scenario:
What question do eleven people in a grant review committee fail to ask?

Consider what Lukas faces at the vote on a behavioral intervention study application. The committee has reviewed the methodology, the sample size, the timeline, and the budget. Eleven members are ready to vote. The meeting has been running for two hours. Lukas has a question that will likely delay the vote and require the lead researcher to consult with a co-investigator. Eleven members are ready to vote. Lukas must decide whether to raise his question before the vote or let the application pass unquestioned. He raises his hand before the vote is called.

'What would a negative result look like for this study, and would we be able to detect it?'

The room slows down. The lead researcher describes what a positive result would look like: a measurable improvement in the behavioral outcome across both cohorts after the 16-week intervention. She describes what a neutral result would look like: no significant difference between cohorts. Then she stops.

A neutral result, it turns out, is as close to a negative result as the study design can produce. The study has no pre-specified threshold for determining that the intervention is actively harmful relative to the control, because the design assumes the intervention is either beneficial or neutral and is not looking for a third outcome.

Lukas asks: 'Is there a plausible mechanism by which the intervention could make things worse? And if so, would this study detect it?'

The lead researcher consults with a co-investigator. The answer is yes: there is a plausible mechanism. The answer is no: the study cannot detect it with the current design.

The committee sends the application back for redesign. The delay is one semester. The redesigned study includes a pre-specified threshold for a harmful outcome and an early stopping rule.
examples.whatToDo: For any study, program, or initiative with a defined success metric, ask explicitly: what would a negative result look like, and would this design detect it? The question is easy to ask and frequently not asked. If the answer reveals a one-sided design, that is a design problem that is cheaper to fix before the study begins than to discover after the results arrive.
examples.whyItMatters: Lukas's question cost the study one semester. Discovering the one-sided design in the results would have cost the institution an unfalsifiable finding worth $850K: a study that can only report a positive or neutral outcome is not testing a hypothesis, whatever else it is doing.

examples.title: At 0830, Min reframes a five-year chronic disease target into annual leading indicators and catches a treatment initiation shortfall in year one

planSpec.domain: public health analyst reframing an oversized population health prediction into testable milestones
planSpec.audience: senior analyst whose department has committed to a five-year chronic disease reduction target with no intermediate checkpoints
planSpec.stakes: a public health initiative with $12M in funding and no mechanism to detect whether it is working before year 5
planSpec.requiredBeat: five-year target decomposed into annual leading indicators; first annual review shows screening uptake on track but treatment initiation 18% below; year-one intervention made possible

examples.scenario:
At eight-thirty in the morning on the day the department's five-year chronic disease reduction target was scheduled to be published, Min walked into her director's office with a question and a revised commitment document.

The five-year target, a 25 percent reduction in age-standardized incidence rates, was ready to publish. Min's question: what would the department do if the rate was only down 10 percent in year five, and how would they know in year two that they were on track?

The director said they would assess in year five and adjust the strategy then. Min said that by year five, the cohort that had not been reached in year two would be five years older and considerably harder to reach. She proposed adding three annual leading indicators to the public commitment: screening uptake rate by year, treatment initiation rate for newly screened patients, and 12-month treatment adherence rate. Each would be reported publicly in the department's annual statistics release.

The target was published with the three annual indicators included.

At the first annual review, screening uptake was 94 percent of the first-year milestone. Treatment initiation was 76 percent of the milestone, 18 percentage points below target. Adherence for those who had initiated treatment was 91 percent.

The bottleneck was initiation, not detection and not adherence. The department redirected outreach resources toward the gap between screening completion and treatment start. The intervention happened in year one. Without the leading indicators, the same information would have been visible in year five, after the window for reaching the year-one cohort had closed.
examples.whatToDo: Before committing to any multi-year target, ask when you would need to know whether you are off track in order to intervene while it still matters. Set milestone checkpoints at that interval, not at the end. If the answer is 'we would need to know in year one,' then a five-year single-number target is not a real accountability structure: it is a five-year exemption from accountability.
examples.whyItMatters: Min's three annual indicators did not make the five-year target more ambitious. They made it checkable at the intervals when checking still mattered. The treatment initiation shortfall in year one was real and addressable. A five-year single-number outcome target would have made the same shortfall invisible until the intervention window had closed.

questions.prompt: Why is public scorekeeping necessary for forecasting to improve across an institution, rather than just across individual forecasters?
choices: Because without public scoring, accuracy and persuasiveness are indistinguishable to the institution, which means the institutional reward system cannot differentiate the two and will default to rewarding whichever is more visible and immediately useful.
Because individual forecasters who track their own accuracy privately tend to be overly self-critical, and public accountability corrects for that downward bias.
Because forecasting accuracy is inherently relative, and individual tracking only shows absolute accuracy rates rather than how a forecaster compares to alternatives the institution could choose.
questions.explanation: The institutional problem with private scorekeeping is that it is invisible to the people who control incentives and reputation. A forecaster who tracks her own accuracy but never publishes it has improved her self-knowledge without changing what the institution rewards. If the institution cannot distinguish accurate forecasters from persuasive ones, it will reward the signals it can observe, which are typically confidence and usefulness to the current decision, not accuracy over time. Public scorekeeping creates the comparison that makes accuracy a visible institutional currency.

questions.prompt: Luke's nonprofit employment re-entry program produces a 61% twelve-month employment retention rate against her expected 75%. She is considering how to present this to the foundation funder. What is the correct approach?
choices: Suppress the 61% figure from external reporting and focus the presentation on the improvement trend expected in the next cohort.
Commission an independent evaluation to validate the 61% figure before presenting it publicly, to avoid presenting a number that may not be statistically reliable.
Present the 61% result publicly, show the component-level breakdown that points to the job-coaching module as the source of the gap, and announce the redesign decision based on what the data shows.
questions.explanation: The 61% figure is what Luke has: an actual measurement against a stated expectation. Suppressing it removes the only number that contains diagnostic information, replacing it with a future promise that has the same evidentiary problem as the pre-tracking testimonials did. Commissioning validation before disclosure delays the accountability feedback loop and suggests that the number is suspect rather than informative. Presenting the figure with the component breakdown turns a potentially uncomfortable data point into a specific, actionable finding that explains both what happened and what comes next. That is what scorekeeping is for.

questions.prompt: Hanna's proposal for a departmental forecast log is resisted by three colleagues who have been making verbal forecasts for years without written records. What does this resistance most accurately reveal?
choices: That the colleagues lack confidence in their own forecast quality and prefer to avoid being compared to peers who may be more analytically skilled.

That these colleagues have built professional reputations in an environment without outcome accountability, and a public forecast log would create a visible comparison between them that their careers had previously been protected from.
That the department's leadership is not committed to evidence-based policy, which is a cultural problem requiring a broader organizational change effort before a logging system can work.
questions.explanation: The three colleagues who resisted Hanna's proposal all made verbal forecasts that had never been recorded. Their objections, that accuracy metrics miss analytical depth, that the domain is too complex to score, that there is no evidence tracking improves outcomes, are not obviously wrong as abstract claims. But each objection has the structural feature of protecting a position that would be exposed if scoring began. The resistance is not evidence of incompetence: it is the rational response of people whose standing was built in an environment where the comparison Hanna was proposing did not exist. Codman's colleagues had the same response for the same structural reason.

questions.prompt: Pablo's strategy team switches from a single annual revenue forecast to a five-component forecast. What does the first quarterly review, showing 2 of 5 components on track and 3 off, enable that the single-number approach did not?
choices: It enables the board and the strategy team to diagnose which components of the business are causing the miss and what specifically changed, rather than only observing that the total number moved.
It enables the strategy team to aggregate the component errors in a statistically principled way, producing a more accurate total forecast than a single-number approach would have generated.
It enables more nuanced communication with the board about the complexity of the business environment, improving the board's understanding of forecasting's inherent limitations.
questions.explanation: The single-number approach produces one signal when the forecast is off: the number missed by a certain percentage. That signal does not distinguish between a systematic model error and an unexpected external event, and it provides no direction for where to focus correction. The five-component breakdown produces five signals, each independently traceable to a specific driver. When three components miss for structurally different reasons, the diagnoses differ and so do the appropriate responses. The first quarterly review does not make the forecast more accurate; it makes the miss legible, which is a precondition for correcting the right thing.

questions.prompt: Devon reviews 140 expert predictions and finds that only 68 of them are specific enough to score. What does the 72-prediction unscorable pool most directly reveal?
choices: That the 72 contributors were deliberately vague to avoid accountability, which represents a systemic editorial culture problem requiring a structural intervention beyond a contributor ranking system.
That 72 of the predictions covered events that had not yet resolved at the time of Devon's review, and those predictions should be rescored once their outcomes are known.

That more than half of the publication's expert predictions were structured in ways that could not be shown to be wrong regardless of how events turned out, which means those predictions provided no accountability to readers even when they appeared authoritative.
questions.explanation: Vague predictions are not necessarily the result of deliberate evasion. They are often the natural output of expert communication in domains where precision is uncomfortable or where the editorial culture does not demand specificity. But the functional effect of vagueness is the same regardless of the intent: a prediction that cannot be scored cannot be shown to be wrong, which means it provides no accountability and no information for distinguishing skill from confidence. The 72 unscorable predictions had been published as expert forecasting. Devon's review revealed that they were something different: authoritative-sounding positions that were structurally exempt from the accuracy check that would have made them genuinely informative.

questions.prompt: Hanna, a policy analyst, reviews her private forecast log and discovers that her stated confidence has averaged 88% on predictions she got wrong, nearly identical to the 85% she stated on predictions she got right. When she proposes a departmental forecast log where predictions and accuracy would be tracked publicly, three colleagues with long verbal forecasting careers object. What explains why this proposal is met with resistance even though it would improve the department's forecast quality?
choices: Because decision-makers are cognitively biased toward confident-sounding information, making them systematically susceptible to persuasive forecasters regardless of any track record that might be available.

Because without scorekeeping, accuracy and persuasiveness are indistinguishable to the institution, and persuasive forecasters are more immediately visible and useful to the people who control reputation and rewards.

Because accurate forecasting typically involves expressing uncertainty and acknowledging limits, which makes it less suitable for the motivational and coordination functions that organizational communication often serves.
questions.explanation: The institutional default is not a product of cognitive bias in isolation: it is a product of measurement absence. Cognitive bias may explain why people find confident-sounding forecasts attractive, but it does not explain why institutions reward persuasive forecasters over accurate ones when both are available. The structural explanation is simpler: when there is no scorekeeping, the institution cannot distinguish them. It can observe confidence, fluency, and usefulness to the current decision. It cannot observe track record. In that environment, the forecaster who optimizes for immediate usefulness will consistently be rewarded over the one who optimizes for accuracy, not because accuracy is less valuable but because it is invisible.

questions.prompt: What makes a forecast question too large to be genuinely accountable, and what does Codman's End Result System model for solving it?
choices: A question is too large when it involves too many interacting variables to model cleanly; Codman's system models the value of reducing a complex outcome to a single trackable summary number.

A question is too large when it spans more than a single year; Codman's system models the value of regular annual review cycles that check forecast accuracy before the forecaster's attention has fully moved to other topics.

A question is too large when its outcome cannot be distinguished from 'the world changed under us,' making any miss ambiguous; Codman's End Result System models tracking individual case outcomes specifically enough that each failure or success is attributable and not absorbed into an aggregate.
questions.explanation: The accountability problem with large questions is not their time horizon or their variable count: it is the ambiguity of their outcomes. A question whose answer, when wrong, can always be explained as 'conditions changed' is not a testable question: it is a position with a built-in escape hatch. Codman's system tracked individual patient outcomes with enough specificity that each case was attributable: the failure was this procedure, on this patient, at this date, with this complication. That specificity is what made the End Result System threatening to his colleagues. Aggregate surgical outcome statistics, then as now, can be interpreted as reflecting case mix rather than skill. Individual case tracking makes that interpretation harder to sustain.

questions.prompt: What is the superquestioner's contribution to forecasting, and why is it as important as the superforecaster's contribution?
choices: The superquestioner frames a question with enough specificity that the resulting forecast can be checked: a specific enough claim, a defined outcome, and a resolvable date; without those elements, even accurate forecasting cannot be detected as accurate.
The superquestioner challenges the premises of an existing forecast by identifying which assumptions are most sensitive to future shocks, improving calibration before the forecast is submitted.

The superquestioner aggregates multiple forecasters' views into a single consensus estimate, using structured elicitation to reduce the anchoring and social pressure effects that individual forecasting is prone to.
questions.explanation: A forecast is only as accountable as the question that prompted it. A vague question produces a forecast that cannot be checked: it can be interpreted as correct regardless of the outcome, which means it provides no information and no accountability. The superquestioner does the upstream work that makes the downstream forecasting legible: they define what counts as a yes, specify the resolution date, and eliminate the escape hatches that vague framing creates. Devon's review of 140 expert predictions found that 72 could not be scored because the questions were not specific enough. The superquestioner's role is to prevent that outcome before the forecast is made.

questions.prompt: A public health department commits to a five-year chronic disease reduction target with no intermediate milestones. An analyst proposes adding annual leading indicators to make year-one progress visible. A program director objects that the indicators are imperfect proxies and will create confusion about what the department is actually trying to achieve. Who is correct?
choices: The program director is correct: imperfect proxies introduce noise into the accountability system and may lead to costly year-one interventions based on false signals, which is worse than waiting for the clean five-year outcome.

The analyst is correct: a five-year single-number target with no intermediate checkpoints cannot be intervened on if it starts failing in year one, while imperfect annual indicators that trigger early action are more valuable than a clean year-five number that reveals failure after the intervention window has closed.

Both are partly correct: the department should use the leading indicators for internal management decisions but not publish them externally, to preserve external accountability without creating public confusion about the proxies' relationship to the actual target.
questions.explanation: The program director's objection is formally correct: leading indicators are proxies and all proxies are imperfect. But the objection assumes that the alternative to imperfect early indicators is a clean and reliable five-year outcome. The actual alternative is a five-year period during which no information is generated about whether the program is working. Min's department discovered that treatment initiation was 18 percentage points below target in year one. That discovery was only possible because the annual indicators were in place. Without them, the same shortfall would have been visible in year five, by which time the year-one cohort would have aged five years and the intervention would have been far more costly. An imperfect signal that arrives when action is still possible is more valuable than a perfect signal that arrives after the action window has closed.

reviewCards.front: What is Codman's End Result System and what did it reveal about institutional accountability?
reviewCards.back: Codman tracked his own surgical outcomes for years, recording complications and failures, and presented them publicly at medical society meetings. His hospital found this threatening and asked him to leave. The system he built became the foundation of modern surgical outcome auditing. His career demonstrated that measurement which can prove you wrong is more threatening to an established institution than measurement that can only confirm what is already believed.

reviewCards.front: Why does public scorekeeping threaten institutional reputations even when it helps institutional outcomes?
reviewCards.back: Reputations built without outcome accountability are built on persuasiveness, confidence, and social standing rather than track record. Public scorekeeping creates a comparison that those reputations have been protected from. The people who resist scorekeeping most strongly are not usually the ones who know their accuracy is poor: they are often the ones who have never had to find out, and who have the most to lose if they do.

reviewCards.front: What makes a forecast question too large to be accountable, and how does decomposition fix it?
reviewCards.back: A question is too large when, after the outcome, you cannot distinguish between 'the forecast was wrong' and 'the world changed under us.' That ambiguity makes the miss uninformative about the forecaster's model. Decomposition breaks the large question into component sub-questions, each with its own trackable indicator and checkpoint date. Each component can be scored independently, and a miss on one component can be distinguished from a miss on another, making the diagnosis specific enough to improve the next forecast.

reviewCards.front: What is the superquestioner's role, and why does it matter as much as the forecast?
reviewCards.back: The superquestioner frames a question specifically enough that the resulting forecast can be checked: a concrete claim, a defined outcome, and a resolvable date. Without that framing, even accurate forecasting cannot be detected as accurate. The superquestioner does the upstream work that makes the downstream forecasting legible. More than half of the expert predictions Devon reviewed were too vague to score, which meant they were unaccountable regardless of how they turned out.

reviewCards.front: Why is an imperfect annual indicator more valuable than a clean five-year target with no intermediate checkpoints?
reviewCards.back: A five-year target with no intermediate checkpoints cannot trigger an intervention until the target period has ended, by which time the opportunity to reach the year-one cohort has closed. An imperfect annual indicator that reveals a shortfall in year one is less precise but arrives when action is still possible. A signal that arrives when intervention matters is worth more than a cleaner signal that arrives after the intervention window has closed, even if the cleaner signal is more reliable.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before making any significant forecast or commitment, ask three questions: Is this question specific enough to score? If I am wrong, will I know what went wrong? Have I broken this into component sub-questions with their own checkpoints? If the answer to any of these is no, reframe the question before making the forecast.

ifThenPlans.context: Before your organization makes a public commitment to a multi-year outcome target
ifThenPlans.plan: If the target spans more than one year, then add at least two annual leading indicators to the public commitment. Define in advance what each indicator means and what threshold would trigger a review. If you cannot define those things before committing, the target is not specific enough to be a real accountability structure.

ifThenPlans.context: When a forecast or prediction is being made verbally without a written record
ifThenPlans.plan: If the forecast will affect a significant decision, then write it down with a date, a stated confidence level, and a resolution criterion. Even a private record is more useful than no record. A verbal forecast with no record is not a forecast: it is a position that can be retrospectively reinterpreted to match whatever happened.

ifThenPlans.context: When a program or initiative has been running for more than one year without outcome tracking
ifThenPlans.plan: If there is no longitudinal tracking system, then build the simplest one that would detect the most important failure mode. The system does not need to track everything: it needs to track the thing that would tell you whether the program is doing what you believe it is doing.

ifThenPlans.context: When reviewing a study design, program design, or forecast methodology
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask: what would a negative result look like, and would this design detect it? If the design can only report a positive or neutral outcome, it is not testing a hypothesis. The question is easy to ask and frequently not asked. The cost of asking it before the study begins is a semester. The cost of discovering it in the results is an unfalsifiable finding.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, find one prediction or forecast your organization has made publicly in the past year that has not been reviewed against its outcome. Score it: was it right, was it wrong, and how confident were you when you made it? If you cannot score it because it is too vague, that is itself a finding: write down what would have made it scoreable, and use that specification for the next forecast you make.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one forecast from your log against its outcome if it has resolved. Record the result: right or wrong, confidence level stated versus accuracy achieved. After a month, look at the pattern. The gap between your average stated confidence and your actual accuracy rate is the calibration problem you should work on first.

memorableLines.text: The 61 percent was not a failure. It was a number she could work with. The testimony had only been a number she could present.
memorableLines.why: It captures the entire chapter's thesis about scorekeeping in three sentences. The contrast between 'work with' and 'present' is the difference between accountable and performative forecasting.

memorableLines.text: Codman tracked his own failures and presented them in public. The hospital found this less comfortable than prestige, and he was shown the door, which tells you more about how institutions treat accountability than about whether his system worked.
memorableLines.why: It names the institutional mechanism precisely: the system worked, and it was still threatening. The final clause carries the lesson without editorializing.

memorableLines.text: A forecast without a score is not a forecast. It is a position. The score is what converts the position into evidence.
memorableLines.why: Three sentences that distinguish forecasting from opining. 'Position' and 'evidence' are the operative contrast, and the one-sentence punch line does the structural work.
